title: Second-Opinion Systems for Rare Diseases: A Scoping Review of Digital Workflows and Networks
content: Rare diseases disseminate expertise across institutions and borders, making structured second opinion systems a pragmatic way to concentrate subspecialty knowledge and reduce diagnostic delays. This scoping review mapped design, governance, adoption, and impacts of rare disease second opinion services across 18 peer-reviewed studies, grouping initiatives by implementation scale. Eight studies operated within European Reference Networks: five were national programs, two were regional systems, and three were international initiatives. Technological approaches were predominantly hybrid, followed by asynchronous and, less often, synchronous models. Across settings, services shared a reproducible backbone, leading to convergent benefits such as faster access to expertise, shorter decision times, and frequent clarification or modification of diagnostic and therapeutic plans. Recurrent enablers included role-based governance, explicit consent and auditability, helpdesks, targeted training, and the explicit resourcing of panel coordination and expert time. Common barriers involved platform complexity, time-intensive panel creation, uneven incentives, variable interoperability, and medico-legal ambiguity outside ERNs. Evidence gaps include prospective, patient-level outcomes, equity and experience measures, comparative effectiveness, costs, and mature connectivity with electronic health records. Overall, systematized second-opinion services for rare diseases are feasible and clinically relevant. Scale depends on usability, incentive alignment, and pragmatic interoperability, which progresses from registries toward bidirectional connections.
